summary:
Batman province stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward trans people has been formalised as state policy rather than left as residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, including 299 detention decisions — 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record — alongside systematic intrusion into the privacy of LGBT people.

A leaked draft omnibus justice package circulated in October 2025, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality. The draft would criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to four years in prison, raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 on a requirement of permanent infertility, and punish health professionals who carry out such care. Human Rights Watch called the draft one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades, and 15 Turkish LGBT groups together with the Turkish Medical Association oppose it. The measure had not been passed when reported, but authorities have acted as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy, found that anti-LGBTI+ hostility has become institutionalised as explicit policy. Senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a Year of the Family banner created a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, while regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricted freedom of expression and artistic freedom. The findings were presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen at the report launch.

Street-level enforcement shows how that framework operates against individuals. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafes in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for General Information Gathering background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detained woman stated that police issued no fines but documented them anyway, and observed that the new law had not yet passed even as enforcement was applied to her.

Foreign visitors stopped at such checkpoints must produce original identity documents, and Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents are compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of them classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate. Monitoring by the Truth Justice Memory Center of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025.

Trans prisoners are placed by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Coordinated by Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın, rights groups demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added gender reassignment as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the other option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

The underlying pattern is longstanding. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and stands as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than a statement of current law.
tangentialFactors:
The enforcement data available for Turkey is drawn from Istanbul, the country's largest city, where police conduct general information-gathering checks on trans women in the Beyoğlu district. Batman province has no equivalent published tally, and the Istanbul figures illustrate the national pattern rather than describe conditions specific to southeast Turkey.

Legislative turbulence is a standing feature of the current environment. The 11th Judicial Package was a leaked draft as of late October 2025 and had not been enacted at that point, yet reporting indicates that the prohibitions it contains are being applied in practice ahead of any vote. Visitors should read pending status as an unsettled question of law rather than as an absence of risk.

Official rhetoric supplies the continuity between periods. Human Rights Watch identifies the government's framing of protecting the family and public morals as the basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people, and the Kaos GL 2025 report traces the same language into instructions issued to public institutions under a Year of the Family banner. Human Rights Watch's 2008 findings, while historical, show that beatings, robbery and abuse directed at trans people predate the post-2018 legal changes.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory reports conditions, police practice, healthcare provision or detention in Batman province specifically. The province-level picture here is inferred from national documentation and from Istanbul examples; local enforcement patterns in Batman remain not sourced.

Whether the 11th Judicial Package has since been enacted is unresolved in these sources. It was reported as a leaked draft in October 2025, opposed by 15 LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association, and unpassed at the time of reporting.

The authenticity and final wording of the leaked package, and whether its gender-affirming care provisions were altered before any vote, are unresolved.

It is unresolved whether the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation applies uniformly to all provinces or was prompted by the Kayseri circular as a regional measure; the sources describe a national regulation reported alongside that circular.

Legal opinion that general information-gathering checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights is attributed to experts cited in reporting and has not been established as a ruling against Turkey in these sources.
